title: Teach Microduck to score a goal
text: What you will build  Follow one Microduck, ball and goal through robot learning: experience motion skills, learn simulation and reinforcement learning, observe complete football, explore GR00T imitation and ASPIRE skill composition, then consider new environments.    1 Motion and learning foundations   2 Review the engineered baseline   3 Learn actions with GR00T   4 Organize tasks with ASPIRE   5 Expand environments with Cosmos and Isaac     By the end, you can   Explain mechanisms, actuators, observations, actions and rewards.  Explore fixed policies and learning with Isaac Lab, Newton and Isaac Sim.  Distinguish engineered pipelines, VLA actions and task agents.  Adapt the SO-101 data workflow to Microduck demonstration/action requirements.  Design variation and held-out evaluation; distinguish readiness from task success.     Course route      Chapter  Task      Chapter 1  Meet Microduck: play football first    Chapter 2  Mechanism and control timing    Chapter 3  Learning to walk    Chapter 4  Adapt walking to slopes    Chapter 5  Explore community movement skills    Chapter 6  From engineered pipelines to intelligent robots    Chapter 7  Teach GR00T from demonstrations    Chapter 8  Organize tasks and accumulate skills with ASPIRE    Chapter 9  From one field to more environments

title: How to take this course
text: Choose a learning path      Path  What you do  What you need      Observe  Read, inspect the 3D assembly, watch demonstrations, and answer checks.  A modern browser    Use fixed models (recommended)  Copy terminal commands, run simulation, and record observations.  A prepared GPU environment    Practice training  Add your own training, export, and evaluation.  Additional runtime and disk space      Start with the demonstrations, then optionally practice training in Chapters 3 and 4. Chapter 6 is an overview; Chapters 7–9 explain frontier methods and integration requirements without new framework installation or large-model training. All reading and browser interactions work without a GPU.    Prerequisites   Open a Linux terminal, change directories, and copy multiline commands.  Read basic Python functions, arrays, and parameters. Prior PPO knowledge is not required.  Understand positions, angles, and velocities; robot coordinate frames are introduced in the course.    About your training results  Your checkpoint is a practice artifact. Later chapters explicitly use the course models in  models/ ; they never select the latest training run automatically. Using your own policy requires an explicit checkpoint and a new evaluation.     A useful lab routine   Read the expected result before running a command.  Run commands from the repository root. Use a new output directory for every run.  Keep the command, seed, and result—including failures.  Answer the chapter check before moving on.   Reading and exercise durations are planning estimates, not training-time guarantees. The first launch may download assets, compile kernels, and populate rendering caches.

title: Prepare your environment
text:
Runtime requirements  The reference environment is Ubuntu 24.04 on DGX Spark (aarch64), Python 3.12, Isaac Sim 6, and pinned Isaac Lab / Newton revisions. Simulation uses Newton’s native actuator path. Other GPUs or versions may run, but the course results do not automatically apply to them.  You need an NVIDIA driver, a GPU-enabled graphical desktop, Git, Docker, and network access to NVIDIA package sources. None of these are required for reading the website. Review the Isaac Sim license before installing the simulator.    Download the course and models  Open a terminal in the directory where you want to keep the course, then run the commands below to clone and enter the repository.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    mkdir -p "$HOME/microduck"
cd "$HOME/microduck"
git clone https://github.com/NV-DLI/Microduck-Workshop.git
cd Microduck-Workshop
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The models are included in the repository, so no Hugging Face login is required. The verification command checks every model’s SHA-256. Continue only when all files match. Course weights and student outputs are stored separately.    Workspace    Microduck-Workshop/
├── web/          # HTML course
├── lab/          # simulation and learning code
├── models/       # fixed course models
├── scripts/      # lab entry points
└── outputs/      # your runs (created when needed)      Prepare the simulator  First prepare system tools. The commands below install Git, Python virtual-environment support, and video encoding. Set up Docker using its  Ubuntu instructions ;  docker info  should show server information without a permission error.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git python3-venv ffmpeg
docker info
export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600      Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py setup
python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor     setup  prepares the pinned runtime. If you already have a matching Isaac Lab checkout, bind it using  --isaaclab /path/to/IsaacLab .  doctor  checks Python, models, GPU, the desktop display setting, and navigation dependencies. Resolve failed checks before continuing.   Launch from your desktop terminal  Run GUI commands in a terminal on the GPU machine’s desktop. The website provides lessons and commands; Isaac opens in its own window. On the first launch, allow shaders and assets to finish loading.     Before you continue  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx    Expected result: input and output names, tensor shapes, and model identity. If the GPU is unavailable, use the troubleshooting page before proceeding. Keep the pinned physics backend and model combination.

title: Meet Microduck: play football first
text:
A small robot that learns new skills  Microduck is an open biped from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face with 14 actuated joints. Start with the official walking and right-foot kick ONNX policies in Isaac Sim, then learn how Isaac Lab trains and evaluates new skills.    Open the pitch and try the keyboard      Walk toward the ball, stop, then switch to the right-foot kick.   Complete  setup  and run the command below from the repository root. Click the Isaac Sim window to focus it. The robot, ball and goal use the same dimensions and physical settings as the autonomous task. Use an English keyboard input mode so an IME does not consume movement keys.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py manual \
  --seconds 600 \
  --output outputs/manual-football-01        Key  Action      W / S  Forward / backward    A / D  Step left / right    Q / E  Turn left / right    Release movement keys  Stand with zero velocity command    Space  Right-foot kick, then stand    R / Esc  Restart / exit      Walk toward the ball, stop with the ball in front of the right foot, and face the goal before pressing Space. Reposition after a miss; press R after a fall. You choose the target and direction; the policies coordinate the joints.  Default standing is the walking policy responding to zero movement commands. Getting up after a fall, sitting and rolling are separate skills. The keyboard lab starts its policy on the contact surface. Chapter 6 additionally gates autonomous detection on settled body motion and observations.    Try a gliding shot on passive wheels  This run uses the roller model from initialization to the end. Its four wheels are passive; the same 14 servos propel, steer and brake through leg posture. It never switches to walking or invokes a leg kick. First observe coasting after key release, then practise slowing early so the ball enters the goal while the robot stops before it.  Close the previous scene, then run the command below in the same terminal.  --locomotion rollers  selects the roller physics model and fixed actor, writing to a new output directory.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py manual \
  --locomotion rollers \
  --seconds 600 \
  --output outputs/manual-rollers-01        Key  Meaning in roller mode      W  Push forward    S  Brake briefly and observe; holding it can reverse motion    Q / E  Turn left / right    Release keys  Coast; this does not guarantee a stop    Space  Run a bounded gliding-shot helper; no leg kick    R / Esc  Reset / exit; A and D do not strafe      Use W, Q and E to bring the ball in front of a wheel, then brief S presses to control approach speed; after alignment, you can also try the Space helper. The roller push input is not a velocity target in metres per second. Compare the modes: a walking shot settles before kicking; a gliding shot transfers momentum through moving contact and then brakes.  Roller mode initializes in a stationary roller posture. Official tyre visuals, mass and inertia are retained; rolling contacts use cylinders 30 mm in diameter and 7.6 mm wide, simplifying the rounded shoulders. Keyboard, football and slope roller experiments share this configuration. Real tyre friction and deformation remain uncalibrated.    How Isaac Sim builds the experiment   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Scene to motion           USD scene  Robot, pitch, ball and goal     Physics  Mass, contact and motors     Policy and input  Keys → ONNX → joint goals      Scene to motion  ×   USD scene  USD places the robot, ball and goal in a shared space. Geometry and materials also affect camera images.    Physics  Mass, inertia, friction and colliders determine contact and motion. Identical appearances can have different physics; realism alone does not validate dynamics.    Policy and input  Keyboard requests specify motion; the ONNX policy converts observations and commands into joint targets. Moving the ball changes the task, not the policy weights.      Rendering, physics and policy have separate roles. A different skill reuses the scene; a different ball position reuses the walking actor.   The robot USD includes joints, collision geometry and inertial properties. The ball has a 5 cm radius and 30 g mass; the goal opening is 38.8 cm wide. Isaac Sim provides the scene and rendering; Isaac Lab configures the Newton physics backend.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    cfg.scene.ball = RigidObjectCfg(
    prim_path="{ENV_REGEX_NS}/Ball",
    spawn=sim_utils.SphereCfg(
        radius=0.05,
        mass_props=sim_utils.MassPropertiesCfg(mass=0.03),
        collision_props=sim_utils.CollisionPropertiesCfg(),
        rigid_props=UsdPhysicsRigidBodyCfg(rigid_body_enabled=True),
    ),
    init_state=RigidObjectCfg.InitialStateCfg(pos=(0.0, 0.0, 0.05)),
)
# Apply the shared official-ball asset, goal and floor materials.
scene_profile = configure_football(cfg, style="A")      Fix the scene and hardware contract  The indoor scene uses a 1 × 1.6 m mat, a secured steel-mesh goal measuring 40 cm wide × 20 cm deep × 25 cm high, and an official black-and-white ball with a 10 cm diameter and 30 g mass. This supports short approaches and shots, not arbitrary obstacle avoidance in a confined space. With an assumed 6 mm frame diameter, post centres are 39.4 cm apart and the clear opening is 38.8 × 24.4 cm. Localization uses centre spacing; scoring uses the clear opening.  Choose two football graphics, pale marble or brown wood within the same 1 × 1.6 m area, robot and lighting. The fixed steel-mesh goal has trapezoidal sides and a sloping back, following the product photo. Frame and wires collide; the floor is a rigid plane without foam compression or raised edges. Different textures do not imply calibrated physical friction for each real surface.      A: striped football pitch; B: plain football pitch; C: pale marble; D: brown wood. The same pose isolates appearance; these are not four task outcomes.   The robot uses official Microduck CAD with backlash and full-body collisions. The course pins the XL330 BAM actuator fit, 200 Hz physics and 50 Hz actor updates. The walking actor controls 14 of the 15 physical servos; it does not independently drive the mouth. Full-body collision geometry allows the head, legs and battery to rest on the ground after a fall.  This is a versioned simulation configuration. The camera corresponds to GC2093, but simulation samples at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz with an uncalibrated 70° horizontal field of view. ToF and body IMU models also contain approximations. This does not establish parity with every latest firmware or hardware error, nor validate full deployment on RK3566. Check the real hardware revision, voltage, joint offsets, lens parameters and end-to-end delay before transfer.  The robot uses official CAD, base mass/joint parameters, motor fits and whole-body collision shapes. The displayed board shape comes from Pi Zero 2 W CAD, while Beta software targets RK3566. Distinguish mechanical appearance from the actual electronics revision.    How walking mode switches between gait and kick policies      File  Size  Role      walk.onnx  793,705 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Walking and standing    kick-teacher.onnx  793,685 bytes, about 0.79 MB  Right-foot kick      The walking and kicking combination retains the fixed official weights used in the existing task validation; those files are not the latest browser walking weights. The roller lab uses the official browser roller model. Hardware correspondence, policy identity and task success require separate checks.                                                                                                         Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    # Read the state once per policy step, then select the active skill.
obs = env.observation_manager.compute(update_history=True)["policy"]
action = walk(obs)

if kick_start is not None:
    phase = (step - kick_start) * 0.02
    weight = 1.0 if phase < 0.14 else max(0.0, 1.0 - (phase - 0.14) / 0.12)
    if weight:
        action = torch.lerp(action, kick(obs), weight)

# The action manager maps network outputs to joint targets.
env.action_manager.process_action(action)    The lab holds the kick for 0.14 s and blends back over 0.12 s. This is a handoff setting, not retraining of the official weights. Small policy files do not imply a small simulator memory footprint.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx      Who decided the next step?   Check your understanding  Which decisions did you make for the robot?   Show explanation  You identified the ball and goal, estimated distance, selected a route and stance, and decided when to kick. Chapter 6 shows an engineered pipeline; Chapters 7–9 explore learned policies and task agents.    Next, inspect the mechanism and the timing between policy and physics.

title: Mechanism and control timing
text: From assembly to components  Microduck is a small biped. Its legs support and move the body, the neck directs its view, and the trunk houses computing, power, and connections. Visual meshes describe appearance. Joints and collision geometry describe permitted motion and contact. These play different roles in simulation.       Open interactive model    Assembled   Exploded  Reset view    Click a part or its label to inspect it  Left-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom. Use the slider to separate the parts.    Move the separation slider to inspect the leg and head servos. Click their labels to identify the driven joints, then inspect the camera, controller board and battery. Reset to trace the leg joints.   Hardware revision and simulation joints  There are 15 servos: five per leg, four for the head and neck, and one for the beak. The policy drives 14 joints; the beak remains fixed. The CAD retains a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W board mesh; this is not the current Beta RK3566 electronics configuration. Chapters 6–7 connect camera, ToF and IMU data to task observation and learned policies.     Parts, joints, and degrees of freedom  A pen held at its tip can rotate in several directions, while a hinge normally rotates around one fixed axis. Robot joints impose similar constraints. A degree of freedom is an independent variable needed to describe permitted motion; a component count describes physical pieces. The 70 components in this viewer do not imply 70 policy actions.      Region  Active joints  Main role      Each leg  Hip yaw, roll, pitch; knee; ankle: 5 joints  Support the body and place the foot    Neck and head  Neck pitch; head pitch, yaw, roll: 4 joints  Orient the camera and head    Beak  Physical servo; not controlled by this policy  Shown in 3D model, excluded from the 14-action interface      Select a hip servo and inspect its output shaft and nearby bearing. The servo controls an active angle, the bearing supports rotation, and brackets connect adjacent joints. Material, shape, and assembly clearance affect motion. The viewer preserves 3D model detail but does not simulate screw preload, plastic elasticity, or cable forces; it is an anatomy aid rather than manufacturing documentation.    How software moves the mechanism    1 Policy action   2 Joint targets   3 Actuator torque   4 Physics update   5 New observation   A policy does not teleport the robot to a desired position. It outputs actions that become joint targets. Actuators produce torque based on the difference between target and measured state. The resulting motion depends on contact, gravity, inertia, and friction.  The policy runs at 50 Hz and physics at 200 Hz: each action spans four physics steps. Backlash introduces passive joints representing transmission play. Passive joints are not additional policy outputs.    Describe motion with frames      Frame  What is expressed here      World  Pitch, goal, and overall robot position    Body  Forward, lateral, and turn commands; ball relative to the robot    Camera  Image rays and detected target directions    Joint-local  A joint’s axis and angle       Check your understanding  If the head joints stay fixed, is the camera image necessarily stable?   Show explanation  No. Body pitch and roll move the neck and camera. Image stability depends on camera orientation relative to the world, not only on joint angles.      Exercise: trace one load path  Start with the assembled model. Trace a path from the left foot through the ankle, shin, knee, thigh, and hip. Ground support reaches the body through this chain. Explode the assembly and select the servos and brackets around a joint. Identify the fixed housing and the part driven by its output. Explosion offsets are display positions, not physically reachable joint poses.  A servo combines a motor, reduction gears, position feedback, and control electronics. Reaching a target takes time and is limited by torque, speed, friction, and backlash. A policy issuing an angle does not mean the joint instantly reaches it. Chapter 2 observes this difference; Chapter 3 explains how a policy learns around it.   Check your understanding  Does moving the foot farther out in the exploded view change the simulated leg length?   Show explanation  No. The web view explains components. Robot description files define simulated dimensions and joint connections.      What the policy receives and produces  Chapter 1 runs inference with a trained policy. It maps the current observation to 14 joint actions without updating neural-network parameters. Changing the velocity command tests the same model under a different request; it is not training. Choosing a different model file changes the policy.      Observation, in interface order  Width  What it tells the policy      Angular velocity and projected gravity  6  Body rotation and tilt    Relative joint positions  14  Pose relative to the nominal posture    Joint velocities  14  Motion at each joint    Previous action  14  Previous control output and temporal context    Velocity, head, and body commands  3 + 4 + 6  Requested behavior                                                                                                             Observation  61       ⋮  Normalize  Hidden 1  512       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 2  256       ⋮  ELU  Hidden 3  128       ⋮  ELU  Action  14       ⋮  Joint actions  Fully connected · inference every 20 ms · no camera images    Circles show a subset of units; numbers give actual dimensions. The official walking and kick actors share this structure but have different weights. The training critic is not shown.   These values total 61. Reordering joints breaks their meaning even if the input still has 61 entries: the policy might read a knee as a hip. Course entry points preserve ordering, nominal posture, and control timing. Begin by changing commands, duration, and output directories; modify observation construction only after understanding the interface.

title: Learning to walk
text:
One reinforcement-learning loop  The policy receives a vector containing body attitude, angular velocity, joint state, a velocity command, and the previous action. It outputs joint actions, physics advances, and rewards measure progress toward the objective. PPO collects a batch of interactions, updates the policy, and samples again.    1 Observe   2 Sample actions   3 Simulate   4 Compute rewards   5 Update PPO   The environment count is the number of simultaneous robot copies. Iterations repeat collection and optimization. More environments increase parallel sampling and memory demand. A rising training reward means the optimized objective is improving; independent behavior checks are still necessary.    Why PPO looks beyond immediate reward  Lifting a foot can briefly reduce stability while being necessary for forward progress. Reinforcement learning therefore considers return over time rather than just the current reward. A discount factor reduces the weight of more distant rewards, balancing immediate feedback with longer-term consequences.  In PPO, the actor chooses actions and the critic estimates future return. An outcome better than the critic expected receives a positive advantage estimate, encouraging a higher probability for the corresponding action; a worse outcome does the opposite. PPO limits how far an update moves from the old policy to reduce abrupt changes. It does not guarantee that every update improves real task success.  A critic may receive additional simulation information to evaluate trajectories, but the deployed actor must depend only on observations available at runtime. A simulator knowing exact body velocity does not imply that hardware has a perfect velocity sensor. Keep training or scoring ground truth out of the deployed controller.  When designing rewards, list desired behaviors and then consider shortcuts. Rewarding ball motion may encourage body collisions; rewarding stillness may discourage walking. Track both goals and constraints: velocity error, episode length, falls, joint limits, and contact type. This chapter practices the training loop; Chapter 6 tests the complete task definition.    Run a short training exercise    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 64 \
  --iterations 20 \
  --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-01    This is a workflow exercise, not a promise that 20 iterations will learn to walk. Expected result: terminal progress, a new run directory, checkpoints, and an exported policy. Observe loss, return, and episode length without committing to a long training run.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py tensorboard \
  --logdir outputs/student-walk-01 \
  --port 6006    Open the local TensorBoard address printed in the terminal. Compare reward with episode length. If reward grows while episodes remain short, consider whether the objective rewards a brief action followed by a fall.  Current practice uses full-body contacts, including the head and legs during falls. New outputs are separate experiments; historical learning curves retain their original configuration. Training does not render frames; policy playback uses the shared RTX lighting and materials.    From a smoke run to a longer training run  The 20-iteration exercise checks the pipeline, not convergence. A longer run below uses 1024 environments for 2500 iterations in a new output directory. Judge convergence with curves and independent evaluation, not iteration count alone.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 1024 --iterations 2500 --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/walking-training-01    Use TensorBoard to compare reward, episode length, falls and velocity error. Use the short-run export in the next section, or explicitly select outputs/walking-training-01/exported/policy.onnx after this longer run. Neither changes the official model.    Explicitly test your own policy  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model outputs/student-walk-01/exported/policy.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-test-01    Here you deliberately select your own model. Compare support, drift, and falls with the official model from Chapter 1. Later lessons still use  models/walk.onnx ; this export does not change their default.   Go further  To increase the budget, choose a new output directory and try, for example, 1,024 environments and 500 iterations. Check available memory and time first. A saved checkpoint is not a qualification result. Evaluate unseen seeds and retain failures.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx --velocity 0.3 0 0 \
  --seconds 12 --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/official-walk-comparison-01    Match command, duration and seed. Compare falls, distance and actual velocity, then test standing at zero command. One moving demonstration is not a complete skill benchmark.    Why domain randomization matters  Real actuators do not have identical friction, delay, and backlash on every run. Varying parameters in training exposes the policy to more conditions. A narrow range can overfit; an excessively broad range can make learning difficult. Randomization can improve robustness but does not replace hardware testing.   Check your understanding  Why is the highest-reward training episode not an independent test?   Show explanation  It contributed to learning or selection, and reward may differ from task success. Independent testing uses predetermined scenarios and success criteria and counts every outcome.      Checkpoints, curves, and independent tests  Practice starts from random parameters rather than the course walking weights. Each PPO iteration gathers trajectories from several environments and then updates the policy. Rewards combine velocity tracking, body attitude, action smoothness, and contact-related terms. Two policies with similar total rewards may obtain them through accurate motion or simply moving less; inspect both behavior and individual reward terms.   initial.pt  records initialization;  model_*.pt  files are checkpoints;  env.yaml  and  agent.yaml  preserve environment and optimizer settings;  exported/policy.onnx  is the inference export. A checkpoint can contain optimizer state, while ONNX normally preserves the inference graph. They are not interchangeable file formats.  Record the training budget, held-out test seeds, and observed behavior. The 20-iteration exercise teaches sampling, updates, saving, and export. A weak practice policy is no reason to replace downstream course defaults. For a larger budget, keep the earlier run, use a new output directory, and state whether you changed environment count, iteration count, or rewards.   Check your understanding  Does saving only ONNX guarantee an exact training continuation?   Show explanation  No. Exact continuation also needs optimizer, normalization and random states, together with matching configuration. Preserve full checkpoints and training settings.      Will a flat-ground skill handle a slope?  You can now collect rollouts, update PPO, export ONNX and test a policy. Will its foot clearance and balance adjustments work on a slope? Predict the outcome, then test the same policy in Chapter 4.

title: Adapt walking to slopes
text:
Start with a testable question  Do not assume the old actor will fail. Hold the policy, command, duration, friction and initial-state distribution fixed while varying slope. Test traversal and balance, not just a single attractive frame.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Terrain generalization           Baseline  Same actor: flat/up/down     Isaac Lab training  Sample parallel terrains     Held-out evaluation  Arrival, falls, speed error      Terrain generalization  ×   Baseline  Test the same actor on flat ground, uphill and downhill to locate its limits. Report the directions separately.    Isaac Lab training  Sample slopes in parallel environments so the policy experiences new contacts and gravity components. Retain flat-ground samples too.    Held-out evaluation  Use starts and seeds excluded from tuning. Compare arrival, falls and speed error under matched conditions.      Evaluate before adapting. Retain flat-ground ability while testing improvements on slopes.     Build a flat–ramp–landing scene  The surface has a 0.35 m flat approach, a 1 m horizontal ramp, and a landing. Positive angles ascend; negative angles descend. A continuous collision mesh avoids unintended steps. Visual materials do not determine contact dynamics.      The darker surface marks the ramp; gold guides show direction and green marks the target. These visual markings do not change contact physics.              Flat: 0.35 m  Ramp run: 1 m  Landing      h(x) = tan(α) · clip(x − 0.35, 0, 1)    Slope α / °       Adjust the slope to compare ascent and descent. Horizontal and vertical scales match; the landing height changes with the angle.    坡面高度  \[h(x)=\tan(\alpha)\,\operatorname{clip}(x-0.35,0,1)\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    slope = math.tan(math.radians(cfg.slope_deg))
xs = [-48.0, 2.35, 3.35, 52.0]
zs = [0.0, 0.0, slope, slope]
vertices = [(x, y, z) for x, z in zip(xs, zs) for y in [-48.0, 52.0]]
origin = np.array([2.0, 2.0, 0.0])    The mesh origin is (2, 2, 0). Subtracting it places the robot at relative x = 0 and the ramp between x = 0.35 m and 1.35 m. Continuous approach and landing support extends across 100 × 100 m so failures do not fall off a small terrain tile. Isaac Lab’s TerrainGenerator and TerrainImporter share this geometry across visualization, physics tests and parallel training.    Test the official walking policy first  Run the official walking policy on a 5° uphill ramp for 20 seconds. Run the command below from the repository root with a new output directory.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --slope 5 --num-envs 1 --seconds 20 --seed 42001 \
  --output outputs/slope-up-05    Without --headless this opens Isaac Sim. Use --num-envs 5 --headless for batched evaluation, and test 0, ±5, ±10 and ±15 degrees in separate output directories. The first 2 s are standing; then the command is 0.25 m/s. Actual speed may differ.  Success requires reaching x ≥ 1.45 m within 20 s with lateral error below 0.3 m and staying upright throughout. A fall remains a failure even if the body later slides across the finish. Reports separate reaching, falls and velocity RMSE.      Slope  Pass  Fall      0°  5/5  0/5    +5°  0/5  0/5    -5°  0/5  5/5    +10°  0/5  0/5    -10°  0/5  5/5    +15°  0/5  0/5    -15°  0/5  5/5      Each angle uses five lightly perturbed starts. Flat trials pass; uphill trials stall without falling; downhill trials fall. This small baseline identifies an adaptation need, not general reliability.    Why flat-ground experience may not transfer  A slope changes foot clearance, gravity along the surface and usable friction. Insufficient clearance or propulsion can stall ascent; downhill landing and balance changes can cause falls. Survival alone misses stalled traversal.    Continue learning across terrain types  Keep the official ONNX unchanged. Initialize a new actor from its weights and normalization, with a fresh critic and optimizer. Mix 25% flat terrain with ascending and descending terrain. Verify initial actor parity before learning.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --num-envs 256 --iterations 1000 --seed 43001 \
  --output outputs/terrain-training-01    Training slopes are tan(α), not degrees: 0.03–0.22 is about 1.7°–12.4°. Training uses pyramidal and inverted slopes; evaluation uses straight ramps and separate seeds.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    sub_terrains = {
    "flat": MeshPlaneTerrainCfg(proportion=0.25),
    "slopes": HfPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
    "descending": HfInvertedPyramidSlopedTerrainCfg(
        proportion=0.375, slope_range=(0.03, 0.22), platform_width=0.7
    ),
}    The fixed terrain weights retain their original training lineage. Current practice runs use the same full-contact robot as the demonstrations, so their contact configuration differs from the historical training and defines a new experiment. Training is physics-only; inspect exported policies in the shared RTX scene.    Balance and direction both matter   第一步：定义有物理含义的误差  \[e_{\omega}=\omega_z-\omega_z^*,\qquad u=\frac{e_{\omega}}{\sigma}\]    第二步：把误差转换为平滑、有界的奖励  \[r_{\omega}=\exp(-u^2)=\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\omega_z-\omega_z^*}{0.15}\right)^2\right]\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    def yaw_rate_tracking(env, std=0.15):
    # Match the commanded turn rate without penalizing normal roll/pitch motion.
    velocity = env.scene["robot"].data.root_link_ang_vel_b.torch
    target = env.command_manager.get_command("base_velocity")[:, 2]

    # Squared, normalized error gives a symmetric reward in (0, 1].
    return torch.exp(-((velocity[:, 2] - target) / std).square())


cfg.rewards.yaw_precision = RewardTermCfg(
    func=yaw_rate_tracking, weight=4.0, params={"std": 0.15}
)      Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \

You changed the world with Isaac Sim, adapted a policy in Isaac Lab and tested its scope. Next, explore community jumping and balancing tasks.

title: Explore community movement skills
text: What else can the same robot learn?  Community projects train jumping and ball balancing using different tasks, rewards and initial states. These demonstrations come from their original simulation environments and do not establish equivalent Newton or hardware performance.      Community jump demonstration in the original four-times slow motion. Observe takeoff, flight, landing and the standing handoff.       Community ball-balancing demonstration: watch the moving support surface and continuous posture corrections.       Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness      Isaac Sim supplies props and contact geometry; Isaac Lab organizes observations, rewards and reset distributions. Equal observation dimensions do not guarantee compatibility: the jump policy repurposes a command field as a launch trigger.    Define a skill’s boundaries  Walking continuously accepts velocity commands. A kick is a short skill with a start and an end. Integrating it into an autonomous task requires entry conditions, a defined exit state, and a way to stop when conditions are unsafe.      Phase  What to check      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness        Why ONNX files are not interchangeable  ONNX is a model representation, not a universal robot-skill protocol. The walking model takes 61 inputs, while the kicking residual takes 62. Both output 14 numbers, yet they are not interchangeable. Input ordering, additional state, action scaling, teacher blending, and termination conditions are all part of the runtime contract.  Loading a model only establishes that its format is readable. Units, joint order and scaling must match the controller. The  models page  lists the fixed weights and their roles. Chapter 6 shows the complete task assembled from these skills.  Watch the kick in three phases: before it, inspect ball and support-foot positions; during it, identify whether contact comes from the foot or another body part; afterwards, inspect recovery of support. Pause the video in each phase and describe the entry and completion conditions. This is more informative than asking only whether the ball moved.    Describe a skill by its contract  Describe a skill using entry conditions, observations, actions, and exit conditions. A kick requires a useful right-foot ball position, goal alignment, stable support, and fresh target information. Execution combines the kicking teacher with a residual correction. It must then return to a stable standing or walking state; touching the ball alone does not finish the task.  A residual adds a constrained correction to an existing action. This reduces what must be learned from scratch but inherits the teacher’s operating range. Starting a local kick far from the ball does not make it search or approach. Navigation creates a valid handoff state; the skill performs its local action.   Check your understanding  The robot is beside the ball, but its remembered position has expired. Should the kick start immediately?   Show explanation  No. Observe again and confirm the entry conditions. Proximity alone does not guarantee valid inputs.      Executing a skill is not completing a task  We currently tell the robot when to move or kick. Joint and IMU feedback support balance, but the policy does not decide where the ball is or which route to take. Next we review a complete perception/planning pipeline, then consider how learned models can take on more decisions.

title: From engineered pipelines to intelligent robots
text: One field, two ways to score  Start with one simple indoor field: one football mat, background, 10 cm ball and goal. Walking uses a leg kick; skating uses controlled contact. Both must send the whole ball through the goal and finish stably. This chapter requires only observation and reflection.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Engineered control: explicit, checkable stages            Observe targets  Camera, ToF and IMU     Choose an approach  Position and heading     Execute a skill  Walk and kick, or glide     Check the result  Score, recover or stop      Engineered control: explicit, checkable stages  ×   Observe targets  A detector finds the ball and goal in images. Range and attitude help interpret those images; a bounding box is not yet a reachable ground position.    Choose an approach  Ball and goal geometry determines an approach. Standing behind the ball is a human-specified task prior; its world position changes with the targets.    Execute a skill  Walking or skating policies turn movement requests into joint actions. A controller decides when to enter a skill, stop or observe again.    Check the result  Check whole-ball crossing, falls and settling after contact. Completing one stage does not establish complete task success.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   Projection, coordinate transforms and a geometric offset behind the ball turn observations into movement goals. Understanding their purpose is enough here. The walking example uses Nav2/Navfn paths and traversability checks, followed by a custom vision-guided stage controller. Skating uses visual feedback without Nav2. Nav2 is an open ROS 2 navigation framework that can integrate with Isaac ROS perception components. The demonstration uses the Nav2 path.    Watch the walking shot      Walking: observe the goal, approach the ball, align, kick and recover. The observer view follows the simulated trajectory; the inset shows the synchronized camera.   Notice the switches between looking down and adjusting heading. Turning changes the ball position relative to the robot, requiring fresh observations. Residual motion can trigger another alignment cycle. Useful individual skills still need coordinated observation, braking and transitions.    Watch the gliding shot      Gliding: remain on wheels, approach and contact the ball, then brake before the goal. There is no switch to a leg kick. Observer and camera views are synchronized.   Skating must give the ball enough speed while stopping the robot in time. Velocity feedback controls braking, with skating active throughout. This demonstration estimates speed by integrating an ideal IMU; real sensor bias and delay require calibration. Compare the videos: a shared goal requires different actions and final conditions.    How to judge reliable performance  A successful video demonstrates possibility. Reliability needs repeated trials excluded from tuning. On the same field, vary the start, ball position and initial heading modestly. Evaluate walking and skating separately using complete success, falls, repeated observations and time. A goal followed by failed stopping is a separate outcome.  Ask in order: was the target seen, was its position estimated accurately, did the action reach its goal, and did the robot finish stably? Accurate detection alone cannot guarantee the later stages. A successful demonstration does not imply success on every trial.    Let demonstrations and experience do more  Explicit pipelines are understandable and diagnosable, but people must design goals, stages and transitions. Moving the ball elsewhere or tackling a longer task requires new coordination. Could instructions and demonstrations teach the actions, while an agent organizes those abilities?  Next, GR00T explains learning actions from observations; ASPIRE explains organizing and improving skills from execution feedback. These are method-design lessons for Microduck. Focus on the required data, the model’s control role and how to evaluate results. Expand environments after the methods work reliably on one field.

title: Teach GR00T from demonstrations
text: From writing steps to providing goals and examples  Give Microduck the instruction “send the ball into the goal” alongside demonstrations of observations and actions. A vision-language-action model (VLA) connects images, language and robot state to predict what to do next. Language expresses the goal; demonstrations show how this robot can achieve it.  GR00T N1.7 is a foundation model that can be post-trained for a robot and task. General visual knowledge helps interpret situations, but an instruction alone does not teach Microduck balance, skating brakes or kick timing. Compatible action interfaces and task demonstrations remain necessary.    How GR00T 1.7 turns observations into actions   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Images and language provide context; robot state also conditions actions                Images + instruction  See the ball and the goal     System 2  Cosmos-Reason2-2B     System 1  Flow-matching action head     Execute actions  Controller + Microduck     Robot state  Joints, attitude, motion     Observe again  The scene changes as we act      Images and language provide context; robot state also conditions actions  ×   Images + instruction  The camera shows the targets; the instruction specifies the desired outcome. Camera views and preprocessing must match demonstrations. New wording cannot replace missing action coverage.    System 2  The vision-language backbone extracts task-relevant features, such as goal direction. System 2 names this perception/reasoning role; it does not imply a readable plan is returned.    System 1  Conditioned on visual-language features and robot state, the flow-matching head transforms initial noise into an action sequence. It generates actions rather than choosing a sentence from a fixed menu.    Execute actions  The executor handles units, limits and timing. A possible Microduck hierarchy uses VLA velocity/gaze requests above an existing balancing policy. It requires demonstrations labeled with those requests.    Robot state  State describes the current body. Similar images can require different actions while leaning, turning or braking. The state branch jointly conditions the action head with visual-language features.    Observe again  After a short execution, fresh images and state inform the next prediction. This feedback changes inputs; ordinary inference keeps model weights fixed.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   Cosmos-Reason2 is the visual-language backbone used by GR00T 1.7. Chapter 9 discusses Cosmos 3 world models and data generation. These related names refer to different roles in the learning workflow.    Pretraining, fine-tuning and inference      Stage  Inputs and changes  Football interpretation      Pretraining  Broad data develop general representations and action priors  A capable starting point    Post-training / fine-tuning  Robot/task data update selected parameters  Learn Microduck actions and football behavior    Inference  Current observations enter fixed weights; actions come out  Repeated observation and execution      Fine-tuning is a common form of post-training. Freezing selected parameters reduces training cost, but frozen components still perform computation. A training step is an optimizer update, not a robot step or one simulation frame.    Predict a chunk; choose how much to execute  An action chunk predicts H future actions. The executor may apply only the first K before predicting again from a new observation, with K ≤ H. Long execution risks stale actions after the ball moves; very short execution puts more demand on inference and communication.   Nominal command duration  \[T_{\mathrm{execute}} = K / f_{\mathrm{action}}\]   For timing illustration only, five actions at 50 Hz represent 0.1 seconds of command time, excluding inference and network delay. This is not a recommended GR00T training setting. H, K and action rate must fit the data, model latency and closed-loop behavior.  Define what an action means. Joint targets require learning more balance and contact detail; velocity, gaze and skill requests can reuse low-level policies. Either is a research option, but labels, processors and execution must agree. The walking actor’s 14 normalized outputs are neither 14 angles in radians nor velocity commands.    Teach one simple field first   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Reliable demonstrations before scale            Fix the task  One field and movement mode     Record examples  Observations + executed  actions     Train the policy  Learn the action patterns     Evaluate independently  Fresh starts, full success      Reliable demonstrations before scale  ×   Fix the task  Choose one mat and background with fixed ball/goal physics. Develop walking and gliding separately; stabilize one mode before broadening scope.    Record examples  Record instruction, timestamped images/state and labels matching the chosen action level. A high-level VLA learns accepted velocity/skill requests, with joint execution logged separately. Low-level action training uses the values after clipping or correction. Mark waits, resets and failures separately.    Train the policy  Adapt the base model using training examples. Images and actions can have different rates; align timestamps rather than blindly matching row numbers.    Evaluate independently  Keep evaluation starts and trajectories out of training and tuning. Measure scoring and stable completion, time and repeated observations. Low training loss is not closed-loop reliability.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   Good demonstrations require more than eventually scoring. Identical starts leave small deviations uncovered, while repeated hesitation may teach unnecessary movements. First make the traditional method accurate and smooth over a reasonable range of starts on one field, then use it as a demonstration source.    Recovering from drift: HG-DAgger and automated experts  After the first deviation, the policy may encounter observations absent from demonstrations. If skating drifts to one side, imitating a straight approach may worsen the error. Successful trajectories alone often omit recovery from off-course states.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Let the learner try, then supply corrective actions             Learner executes  Notice drift or failure     Expert takes over  Correct from the current  state     Aggregate corrections  Mark ownership and timing     Fine-tune and retest  Evaluate without assistance      Let the learner try, then supply corrective actions  ×   Learner executes  Let the learner visit states it actually encounters rather than only replay ideal trajectories. Triggers may include drift, excess speed or a lost target, before recovery becomes impossible.    Expert takes over  HG-DAgger uses human decisions and corrective actions. A reliable traditional recovery controller can instead provide automated expert corrections: a DAgger-style variant, not human-gated intervention.    Aggregate corrections  Record observations, learner proposals, expert commands, executed actions and ownership. Successful expert segments provide labels; wrong autonomous actions, pauses and resets are not correct demonstrations. Chunks must not cross discontinuous segment boundaries.    Fine-tune and retest  Usually collect with fixed model weights, then fine-tune offline. Evaluate the new policy with intervention disabled. Assisted completion is not independent policy success.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   Automated takeover is worth studying for Microduck because it can reuse validated controls. High accuracy from standard starts is insufficient: the expert must handle moved balls, heading errors, existing motion and briefly lost targets. Improve recovery or stop/reset where it cannot recover; do not train on failed corrections.  A biped cannot simply pause joint commands like a fixed-base arm. Clear stale action queues during takeover, maintain balance or controlled braking, and assign head/body ownership explicitly. If a simulation expert uses exact positions, label that privileged information and exclude it from the future real-robot policy inputs.   Check your understanding  Why do 20 assisted successes not prove the policy has learned?   Show explanation  The expert may have supplied the decisive recovery. Retest without intervention and report intervention frequency and expert recovery separately.      Connect Microduck to a capable computer  Microduck’s onboard computer is not suitable for running a large VLA such as GR00T. A real robot can communicate with a computer equipped with a suitable GPU: the robot streams images and state, the computer runs inference and returns action requests. Choose hardware based on the model, precision and measured latency.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Remote inference with continuous local control and feedback            Robot sensors  Images, state and timestamps     GPU computer  Inference and action requests     Robot executor  Check freshness; balance      Remote inference with continuous local control and feedback  ×   Robot sensors  Preserve sample timestamps and sequence numbers. Do not combine unrelated image and state times as one observation.    GPU computer  Generate actions from the latest valid observation. Network, preprocessing and computation all contribute to end-to-end delay; a fast response can still be based on an old image.    Robot executor  Accept only valid, timely requests. Keep low-level control running; on timeouts or disconnection, use controlled stopping or stable holding instead of stale forward commands.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   A smarter model does not remove control engineering. It predicts actions, while local execution maintains balance, manages freshness and handles interrupted communication. The next chapter lets an agent organize reliable action skills into longer tasks.

title: Organize tasks and accumulate skills with ASPIRE
text: A capable agent needs reliable actions  The VLA addresses actions from current observations. Longer tasks add decisions: find the ball or inspect the goal first, recover after a miss, or move to another target after scoring. A robot agent can organize such decisions by connecting language goals to executable skills.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     The agent organizes the task; controllers keep executing             Task instruction  Send the ball into the goal     Task agent  Choose skills and checks     Motion capabilities  Engineered or learned control     Execution feedback  Observations and outcomes      The agent organizes the task; controllers keep executing  ×   Task instruction  The instruction states the outcome while leaving methods open. Completion needs observable criteria, such as whole-ball crossing and stable termination.    Task agent  The agent sequences defined observation/action tools and handles failures. Its executable abilities are bounded by those tools.    Motion capabilities  Low-level motion responds promptly. Begin with traditional controls and later introduce validated GR00T skills with compatible interfaces.    Execution feedback  Return structured outcomes and relevant images to distinguish missed detection, inaccurate motion and failed stopping. A single success flag rarely explains a useful repair.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.     ASPIRE: try, diagnose, improve and reuse  ASPIRE is NVIDIA’s open robot-skill discovery framework. An agent writes and revises control programs, inspects execution traces, diagnoses failure and tests repairs. Validated experience becomes reusable skills for later tasks. This improves programs and skill knowledge, unlike GR00T training that updates neural parameters.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Execution results determine which experience to retain             Propose a program  Use perception/action tools     Try in simulation  Record observations/actions     Diagnose and revise  Repair based on evidence     Validate and reuse  Keep repeatable skills      Execution results determine which experience to retain  ×   Propose a program  For example: observe, request a short approach, then check ball position. Programs must use real execution tools, not an imaginary always-successful shot command.    Try in simulation  Record observations around tool calls to connect requested turning to actual movement. Simulation enables repeated, bounded experimentation.    Diagnose and revise  If the ball scores but the robot keeps moving, investigate braking and termination; more detection calls may not help. Each repair needs a specific hypothesis.    Validate and reuse  Evaluate on starts not used for repairs, then retain applicability, usage and recovery guidance. Remembering one successful parameter set is not a general skill.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   For Microduck, first validate observation, short movements, controlled stopping and outcome checks on the same simple field, then compose a complete shot. Balancing continues while the agent reasons or waits for network responses. New environments and longer tasks build on those reliable capabilities.    Combining GR00T with ASPIRE      Layer  Question  Football example      ASPIRE / task agent  What to invoke, check and improve  Choose to reposition after observing an offset ball    GR00T / action policy  Which actions fit this observation  Generate approach or contact actions    Local control  How to execute promptly and stably  Balance, limits, braking and timeouts      This hierarchy allows gradual replacement of capabilities without giving a large model every joint at once. Coordinates, timing and units still matter; clear tool interfaces encapsulate those details so the agent can compose them.    Further reading: Agnes Harness  Agnes Harness also organizes robot tasks around models, tools and feedback. Its device integration and plugin design are useful further reading. Compare how tools connect to robots, how results return and how failures inform reuse. ASPIRE supplies this chapter’s main skill-discovery methodology.   Check your understanding  Does unlimited retrying guarantee improving capability?   Show explanation  No. It needs reliable tools, diagnostic feedback, bounded attempts and tests excluded from repairs. Keep improvements that reproduce under evaluation.

title: From one field to more environments
text: Make one scene reliable first  Fix one mat, background and set of props. Establish a reliable traditional baseline, then evaluate independent GR00T execution and ASPIRE skill organization. This order makes failures interpretable: if the original scene is unreliable, adding ten rooms usually makes diagnosis harder.  After reliable handling of fresh starts, modest ball offsets and complete stopping on one field, ask whether the system transfers to another home. Lighting, background, layout and surfaces do vary, but training need not change every factor at once.    Distinguish appearance from action failures      Observed failure  Useful direction  Avoid assuming      Ball is missed under new light  Visual coverage and appearance variation  Random goal materials fix every failure    Ball is seen but approach drifts  Corrections from off-course states  More background images teach recovery    Ball scores but robot cannot stop  Braking, dynamics and delay calibration  Photorealism guarantees stopping    Furniture blocks the route  Layout variation and obstacle-handling skills  Changing floor textures teaches navigation      Domain randomization changes selected training conditions to reduce dependence on one environment. Appearance variation changes images; dynamics variation changes motion. Design them separately. Keep goal-frame material fixed; possible floor expansion includes two football patterns, marble and brown wood.    Cosmos 3: visual variation for an action sequence  Cosmos 3 is an omnimodal family for understanding and generating world-related data. One relevant research path is video transfer: use existing simulation video with controls such as edges, depth or segmentation to generate candidate lighting and interior variations.   Select a module to explore its role and data flow. You can also use Tab and Enter. Swipe horizontally to see the full diagram     Vary appearance and check whether action labels remain valid            Reliable source trace  Images, state and actions     Cosmos 3 transfer  Conditioned visual variation     Check consistency  Geometry, contact and timing     Train and compare  Unaided success in new scenes      Vary appearance and check whether action labels remain valid  ×   Reliable source trace  Source data need correct actions and timing. Restyling a demonstration without braking skill does not add that skill.    Cosmos 3 transfer  Structural controls help preserve layout while appearance changes. Outputs remain candidates: conditioning does not guarantee every frame is correct.    Check consistency  Inspect ball scale, posts, robot shape, contact time and temporal continuity. If a ball moves to the other side of a foot, the old action label may be invalid; reject the segment.    Train and compare  Compare against training without generated data under matched data and compute budgets. Hold out rooms or combinations to evaluate the benefit.      Follow the arrows and select modules for explanations.   Generated video is not a new physics experiment. A prettier goal does not establish executable actions; reliability still needs closed-loop simulation and later hardware tests. Friction, mass and braking-distance changes require physics parameters and measurements.    Composing robots, scenes and tasks  Isaac Lab-Arena separates Scene, Embodiment (robot, sensors and actions), and Task (goals and completion criteria) for compositional evaluation and data collection. Isaac Lab organizes learning environments, Newton advances physics and a renderer produces images. OSMO can orchestrate data generation, training and evaluation workflows.  Combinations require compatible sensors, actions and clear evaluation criteria. Walking and skating are two modes of one Microduck, evaluated separately. Running environments concurrently does not itself produce one policy controlling every robot.    Design an evaluation matrix      Four floors    Three lighting conditions    Three indoor layouts    Walking and skating, evaluated separately   Fresh seeds per combination      This only counts combinations; it launches no simulation or training. Unchecking a factor fixes it to one condition.     Expand one factor at a time  A useful progression is: stable completion on one field → modest lighting variation → new floor appearance → new room layouts → measured dynamics variation. Keep the previous stage as a baseline with the same complete-success criteria. Add visual coverage for perception failures, or revisit corrections and control calibration for drift and braking.   Check your understanding  Do ten restyled backgrounds provide ten times the action experience?   Show explanation  No. Visual conditions expand, but action/state coverage may remain unchanged. Recovery, new routes and braking need corresponding trajectories or corrections.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Start with the environment report  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The first failure is more useful than repeatedly launching a full training run. Check the repository directory, the selected runtime, and all model checks.    Common issues      Symptom  What to check      No GUI window  Use the GPU desktop terminal and check DISPLAY and the driver. A remote text shell is not a graphical desktop.    First launch is slow  Check for downloads and compilation. Allow initialization and avoid starting duplicate instances.    Output directory exists  Choose a new run name and preserve the previous result.    Out of memory  Reduce training environments or detector batch size. Avoid concurrent simulations.    Model hash mismatch  Restore the repository model and check for accidental overwrites.    Practice policy walks poorly  A short run teaches the workflow. Inspect reward, episode length, and evaluation. Continue with fixed models.    Robot stops or does not score  Inspect the task report and observation validity. Stopping can be appropriate when information is missing; it is not a goal.        Inspect a run  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01    When reporting an issue, include the command, seed, environment report, and first error. A success/failure label alone is not enough. Do not include passwords or access tokens.

title: Further learning and references
text: Robotics and simulation  Begin with task observations, actions, and rewards, then explore physics and sensors. Course commands target fixed versions; current documentation may describe newer versions. Check the version before applying changes.    Suggested extensions   Vary the Chapter 3 training budget and compare on the same held-out seeds.  Compare the two Chapter 6 modes: which failures concern observation, action or handoff?  Use Chapter 7 to identify shared data-workflow steps and different action interfaces for Microduck and SO-101.  Use the Chapter 9 counter to plan held-out room evaluation and separate training from test conditions.
